title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXVII
paragraphs:
Now is there civil war within the soul:
Resolve is thrust from off the sacred throne
By clamorous Needs, and Pride the grand-vizier
Makes humble compact, plays the supple part
Of envoy and deft-tongued apologist
For hungry rebels.

Fortunately, Lydgate had finished the evening a loser and left the billiard room with no encouragement to raid the resources of luck. The next day, when he had to pay four or five pounds beyond all his winnings, he felt nothing but disgust with himself. He carried an acutely unpleasant image of the figure he had cut: not merely rubbing shoulders with the Green Dragon’s regulars, but behaving exactly like them. A philosopher who takes to betting looks much like a Philistine doing the same. The chief difference appears afterward, in his reflections, and Lydgate found those thoroughly disagreeable to chew over. Reason showed him how a small change of setting might have enlarged the episode into ruin. Had he entered a gambling house, he could have seized chance with both hands instead of picking it up between finger and thumb. Yet although reason strangled his desire to gamble, the feeling remained that, if he could have been sure of winning enough, he would have preferred gambling to the alternative that was beginning to seem unavoidable.

That alternative was an appeal to Mr. Bulstrode. Lydgate had boasted so often, to himself and others, that he was entirely independent of the banker. He had supported Bulstrode’s plans solely because they let him pursue his own ideas of medical work and public benefit. In their dealings, his pride had been sustained by the belief that he was putting this domineering banker to good social use, despite despising his opinions and often finding his motives an absurd mixture of contradictory impressions. All this had built formidable barriers in his mind against making any substantial request on his own behalf.

By early March, however, his affairs had reached the stage at which men begin explaining that their vows were made in ignorance. What they once called impossible becomes visibly possible. Dover was about to enforce his ugly security. The earnings of Lydgate’s practice disappeared immediately into old debts. If the worst became known, suppliers might refuse credit even for daily necessities. Above all, the image of Rosamond’s hopeless discontent haunted him. He was beginning to see that he must inevitably stoop to asking someone for help. At first he considered writing to Mr. Vincy. But questioning Rosamond confirmed his suspicion that she had already appealed to her father twice, most recently after Sir Godwin’s refusal. Papa had said Lydgate must look after himself. “Papa said that one bad year after another had made him trade increasingly on borrowed money, and he’d had to give up many comforts. With his family expenses, he couldn’t spare even a hundred pounds. He said you should ask Bulstrode, since you’ve always been so close.”

Lydgate himself had indeed concluded that if he must finally ask for an unsecured loan, his connection with Bulstrode offered more grounds than any other for a claim that was not wholly personal. Bulstrode had indirectly contributed to the failure of his practice, and had been greatly pleased to secure a medical partner for his projects. Yet who among us has ever fallen into such dependence without trying to believe in claims that make asking less humiliating? Lately Bulstrode did seem to have lost some interest in the Hospital. His health had worsened, though, with signs of a deep nervous disorder. Otherwise he seemed unchanged. He had always been extremely polite, but from the start Lydgate had noticed a distinct coldness toward his marriage and other private affairs. Until now, he had preferred this to any warm familiarity between them. He postponed his intention day after day. His normal habit of acting on a decision had weakened because every possible decision, and the action it required, repelled him. He saw Mr. Bulstrode often but used none of these meetings for his private purpose. One moment he thought, “I’ll write. Better than talking around the subject.” At another, “No. In conversation I could retreat at the first sign of unwillingness.”

Still the days went by. No letter was written and no special meeting arranged. As he shrank from the humiliation of dependence on Bulstrode, he began growing used to another idea, even less like his remembered self. Of his own accord he considered whether they could follow Rosamond’s childish proposal, which had so often angered him: leave Middlemarch without any plan beyond departure. “Would anyone buy my practice even now, for the little it’s worth?” he wondered. “Then selling our possessions could be treated as a necessary preparation for leaving.”

He still regarded this course as a contemptible surrender of his present work. It would mean guiltily abandoning a real and potentially expanding field of worthwhile action, to begin again with no soundly chosen destination. A practical obstacle also stood in the way: a purchaser, if one could be found at all, might take time to appear. And afterward? Poor lodgings, whether in the greatest city or the most distant town, would not give Rosamond a life that spared her gloom or spared him the reproach of having brought her to it. A man whose fortunes have reached the bottom of the hill may remain there a long time, however skilled in his profession. In the British climate, scientific insight and furnished lodgings are perfectly compatible. The chief incompatibility is between scientific ambition and a wife who objects to such accommodation.

In the midst of this hesitation, an opportunity settled the matter. Mr. Bulstrode sent a note asking him to call at the Bank. The banker had lately shown signs of hypochondria. His sleeplessness was really little more than a worsening of a familiar symptom of indigestion, but he dwelt on it as a warning of approaching madness. That particular morning he wanted Lydgate’s advice immediately, though he had nothing new to report. He listened eagerly to the reassurances, which were equally familiar. As Mr. Bulstrode received medical comfort, mentioning a personal need seemed easier than Lydgate had imagined. He had been insisting that the banker should spend less time on business.

“We can see how even slight mental strain affects a delicate constitution,” Lydgate said, at the point in a consultation where observations begin to move from the individual to the general, “when we consider how deeply anxiety can mark even someone young and vigorous. I’m naturally very strong, but an accumulation of troubles has shaken me badly lately.”

“I suppose a constitution as vulnerable as mine presently is would be especially liable to cholera, should it reach us. Since it has appeared near London, we have every reason to besiege the Mercy-seat for protection.” Mr. Bulstrode did not mean to evade Lydgate’s hint. His fears about himself truly absorbed him.

“At least you’ve done your share in taking practical precautions for the town. That’s the best way of asking for protection,” Lydgate said. The banker’s religious reasoning, with its muddled metaphors and faulty logic, strongly repelled him, the more so because his sympathy seemed deaf. Still, Lydgate’s mind had begun its long-prepared movement toward asking for help and had not stopped. He added, “The town has done well with cleaning and providing equipment. If cholera comes, I think even our opponents will admit that the Hospital’s arrangements serve the public.”

“Indeed,” Mr. Bulstrode replied somewhat coldly. “As for your recommendation that I reduce my mental labors, Mr. Lydgate, I’ve been considering a plan of that kind for some time—a very definite plan. I intend at least temporarily to withdraw from directing much of my business, both charitable and commercial. I’m also considering a change of residence. I shall probably close or let ‘The Shrubs’ and take a house near the coast, with advice, of course, on the healthiness of the location. You would recommend such a measure?”
“Oh, yes,” said Lydgate, sinking back into his chair. He could barely restrain his impatience beneath those earnest pale eyes and that intense self-absorption.

“For some time I’ve felt I should discuss this with you in relation to our Hospital,” Bulstrode continued. “Under the circumstances I’ve described, I must naturally give up any personal role in its management. My sense of responsibility does not permit me to continue devoting large resources to an institution I cannot supervise and, to some extent, direct. If I finally decide to leave Middlemarch, I shall therefore withdraw my support from the New Hospital, apart from the lasting support represented by my having paid most of the building costs and contributed further large sums to its successful operation.”

When Bulstrode made one of his customary pauses, Lydgate thought, “Perhaps he’s lost a great deal of money.” That seemed the likeliest explanation of a speech that had abruptly changed his expectations. He replied—
“I’m afraid it will be almost impossible to replace that loss to the Hospital.”

“Almost,” Bulstrode agreed in the same slow, silvery voice, “unless the plan changes. The only person we can confidently expect to increase her contributions is Mrs. Casaubon. I’ve spoken to her about it and explained, as I’m about to explain to you, the desirability of attracting wider support by changing the system.” He paused again, but Lydgate said nothing.

“I mean joining it to the Infirmary. The New Hospital would become a special extension of the older institution under the same governing board. Their medical management would also have to be combined. This would remove the difficulty of providing adequate support for our new establishment. The town’s charitable efforts would no longer be divided.”
As he paused once more, Mr. Bulstrode lowered his eyes from Lydgate’s face to the buttons on his coat.

“No doubt that solves the question of funds,” Lydgate said with an edge of irony. “But you can hardly expect me to welcome it immediately. One of the first consequences will be that the other doctors disrupt or overturn my methods, if only because they’re mine.”

“As you know, Mr. Lydgate, I greatly valued the opportunity for new, independent work that you have used so diligently. The original plan was very dear to me, subject always to the Divine Will. But since Providence now calls on me to give it up, I submit.”

Bulstrode showed an exasperating skill in this conversation. The muddled metaphors and flawed reasoning about motives that had aroused Lydgate’s contempt could coexist perfectly with a presentation of facts that left him little room to express his disappointment and anger. After thinking quickly, he asked only—
“What was Mrs. Casaubon’s response?”

“That is the further point I wanted to explain,” said Bulstrode, who had prepared his official statement thoroughly. “You know how generous she is. Happily, she has—not a great fortune, I presume, but funds she can readily spare. She tells me that although she has set aside most of those funds for another purpose, she is willing to consider taking my place entirely in relation to the Hospital. She would like sufficient time to think it over. I’ve assured her there is no hurry and that my own plans are not yet final.”

Lydgate nearly said, “If she replaced you, it would be a gain rather than a loss.” But the weight still on his mind checked that cheerful frankness. “Then I suppose I may discuss it with Mrs. Casaubon,” he replied.

“Exactly. That is her express wish. Her decision, she says, will depend largely on what you can tell her. Not immediately, though. I believe she’s about to travel. I have her letter here.” He took it out and read: “‘For the immediate future I have another engagement. I’m going to Yorkshire with Sir James and Lady Chettam. What I decide about some land I’m to see there may affect how much I can contribute to the Hospital.’ So there’s no need for haste, Mr. Lydgate. I merely wanted to let you know in advance what may happen.”

He replaced the letter in his side pocket and shifted his posture as if their business were finished. Renewed hope for the Hospital only sharpened Lydgate’s awareness of the circumstances that poisoned it. If he was going to seek help at all, he must make the effort now, and decisively.

“Thank you for giving me full warning,” he said. His tone was firm, but breaks in his speech showed his reluctance. “My profession matters more to me than anything, and I’ve regarded the Hospital as the best use I can currently make of it. But the best use doesn’t always bring financial success. Everything that has made the Hospital unpopular has also helped make me unpopular as a doctor, along with other causes which I think all arise from my professional enthusiasm. Most of my patients can’t pay. I’d prefer them, if I had no payments to make myself.” He waited briefly. Bulstrode merely bowed and continued looking steadily at him. Lydgate resumed in the same broken manner, as though swallowing something he found distasteful.

“I’ve fallen into financial difficulties from which I can see no escape unless someone who trusts me and my future lends me money without further security. Little of my fortune remained when I arrived. I have no expectation of money from my family. Marriage has made my expenses far greater than I anticipated. At present, a thousand pounds would be needed to put me clear. I mean, to save all my belongings from being sold to meet my largest debt, pay my other debts, and leave a little to keep us ahead on our small income. I’ve found that my wife’s father cannot possibly advance the money. That’s why I’m explaining my position to—to the only other man who might be considered personally connected with my prosperity or ruin.”
He hated hearing his own words. But he had spoken, with unmistakable directness. Mr. Bulstrode answered without either haste or hesitation.

“I’m sorry to hear this, Mr. Lydgate, though I confess I’m not surprised. Personally, I regretted your marriage into my brother-in-law’s family. They have always been extravagant and already owe me a great deal for maintaining their present position. My advice would be to avoid further obligations and a struggle of doubtful outcome. Simply declare yourself bankrupt.”
“That wouldn’t improve my prospects,” Lydgate said bitterly, rising, “even if the thing itself were more pleasant.”
“It is always a trial,” Mr. Bulstrode replied. “But trials are our lot in this world, my dear sir, and a necessary correction. I suggest you consider my advice.”
“Thank you,” Lydgate said, scarcely knowing his own words. “I’ve taken too much of your time. Good day.”
